User segmentation and retention modeling

Finding the behaviors behind fitness retention

I studied how routines, content choices, devices, and challenge response shaped continuing engagement on a digital fitness platform.

4distinct behavioral profiles
50%+of users in the largest opportunity group
Multi weekview of behavior before and after a challenge
One signalconsistency mattered more than a label

The business question

Which members were likely to stay engaged, which members could be activated, and what experience would help each group continue?

My role

I led the analysis from behavioral framing through segmentation, validation, visualization, and recommendations.

01

Four profiles revealed four different relationships with fitness

Some members relied on a stable routine, some explored broadly, some preferred immersive workouts, and the largest group needed help turning short motivation into habit.

02

Profile membership did not explain everything

Returning consistently across weeks was a stronger retention signal than simply belonging to a high activity profile.

03

The challenge created response, not lasting routine

The least active group showed the strongest lift during the event, then lost momentum once the temporary structure disappeared.

Profile A

Shorter workouts, high completion, tablet use, and a structured weekday routine.

Profile B

Mobile use, lower ongoing activity, and the strongest response to the challenge.

Profile C

Longer television workouts, broad weekly participation, and strong loyalty.

Profile D

Desktop use, broad content exploration, and a less predictable routine.

The results in one view

The strongest insights appeared when segment descriptions were compared with what members actually did after the challenge.

50%+

The largest segment was also the largest opportunity

More than half of users sat in the lowest activity group, so even a modest improvement in repeat engagement could reach a meaningful share of the audience.

Highest lift

Low activity did not mean low responsiveness

This group reacted most strongly during the challenge. The response showed that the right moment and structure could activate them.

Low 60% range

The gap appeared after the event

Retention fell back once the challenge ended, pointing to a missing bridge between temporary motivation and an ordinary weekly routine.

Strongest positive signalReturning consistently across weeks
Unexpected risk signalA rigid preference for one workout day

A routine helped when it made exercise repeatable. It became fragile when engagement depended on one exact day that could be disrupted by everyday life.

Unexpected findings that changed the story

The profiles became useful when they revealed why members behaved differently and where a product intervention could change what happened next.

Finding one

Four primary devices aligned with four behavioral profiles

What appeared in the data

Each profile had a different dominant device. Profile A primarily used tablet, Profile B used mobile, Profile C used television, and Profile D used desktop. The pattern remained stable across observation weeks.

Why it mattered

The near one to one correspondence was unexpected because device was only one part of the behavioral data. It suggested that device preference could provide an early clue about a member’s likely profile before a longer activity history exists.

How the business could use it

Device preference could support early segmentation and guide initial onboarding, content recommendations, and messages. It should remain a starting signal rather than a final classification, then be refined as more behavior develops.

Finding two

The least active group showed the greatest activation potential

What appeared in the data

The largest group had the lowest viewing and consistency, yet it produced the strongest challenge response. Engagement dropped again after the event and retention settled in the low sixty percent range.

Why it mattered

These members were not unreachable. They responded when motivation had a clear structure, but that structure ended before a repeatable habit formed.

How the business could use it

A bridge after the challenge could offer immediate follow up, mobile friendly quick content, short recurring challenges, consistency reminders, and visible progress.

The opportunity: convert a strong first response into a routine members can repeat.

Why these results were credible

The analysis separated the behavior used to form profiles from the later outcomes used to test them.

Before

Several weeks of routine, device, content, and engagement behavior formed the profiles.

During

Challenge response showed which groups could be activated by a temporary event.

After

Later activity and retention tested whether the patterns continued beyond the event.

Strategy by profile

One shared campaign would miss the different reason each group engaged.

Profile A

Extend an existing routine with short challenges and low pressure participation.

Profile B

Build continuity with accessible mobile content and a clear path after each event.

Profile C

Offer progression, advanced series, and new goals rather than basic reminders.

Profile D

Turn exploration into a personalized path based on the content they discover.
